parts.stem: Find an equation for the speed \(v_1\) of the car in terms of \(t\).
parts.hint: The car starts from rest and increases speed at a constant rate, so its velocity-time graph is a straight line through \((0,0)\) and \((5,50)\). Find its gradient.

steps.explain: A constant rate of increase means the car’s velocity is linear: \(v_1=mt\), since it starts from rest.
Use this gradient in the line equation.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" viewBox="0 0 360 240" style="max-width:406px"><rect width="360" height="240" fill="white"/><path d="M45 190H320M60 210V25" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60 190L285 55" stroke="#5b4ce2" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 190Q172.5 190 285 55" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M285 55V190M60 55H285" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><circle cx="60" cy="190" r="4" fill="#334155"/><circle cx="285" cy="55" r="4" fill="#06a77d"/><text x="48" y="207" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">0</text><text x="281" y="207" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">5</text><text x="35" y="61" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">50</text><text x="322" y="195" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t (s)</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">v (m/s)</text><text x="140" y="108" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b4ce2">car</text><text x="245" y="150" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#b45309">jet</text></svg>

parts.stem: How far behind the car is the jet after 5 seconds?
parts.hint: Distance travelled is the area under each speed-time graph. Find the car’s triangular area and the jet’s area by integrating \(2t^2\).

steps.explain: The car’s graph from 0 to 5 seconds is a triangle with base 5 and height 50.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" viewBox="0 0 360 240" style="max-width:406px"><rect width="360" height="240" fill="white"/><path d="M45 190H320M60 210V25" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60 190L285 55" stroke="#5b4ce2" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 190Q172.5 190 285 55" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M285 55V190M60 55H285" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><circle cx="60" cy="190" r="4" fill="#334155"/><circle cx="285" cy="55" r="4" fill="#06a77d"/><text x="48" y="207" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">0</text><text x="281" y="207" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">5</text><text x="35" y="61" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">50</text><text x="322" y="195" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t (s)</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">v (m/s)</text><text x="140" y="108" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b4ce2">car</text><text x="245" y="150" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#b45309">jet</text></svg>

steps.explain: Integrate the jet’s speed from 0 to 5 seconds.
Subtract the jet distance from the car distance to find how far behind it is.

parts.stem: After how many seconds does the jet catch up with the car?
parts.hint: Set the distances travelled equal. Integrate each speed from the common starting point, then solve for the positive time after the start.

steps.explain: Integrate the speeds to get distances from the start.
Set distances equal. Exclude \(t=0\), when both were together at the start.
For the later meeting, solve the remaining factor.

questions.stem: Find a primitive of \(3+\frac1x\).
questions.hint: Integrate the constant and use the standard primitive of \(1/x\).

steps.explain: Integrate the two terms separately.
Add the results and the integration constant.

questions.stem: When a valve is released, a chemical flows into a large tank that is initially empty. The volume, \(V\) litres, of chemical in the tank increases at the rate \(\frac{dV}{dt}=2e^t+2e^{-t}\), where \(t\) is measured in hours from the time the valve is released.

parts.stem: At what rate does the chemical initially enter the tank?
parts.hint: Evaluate the given rate at the start, \(t=0\). Remember that both exponentials equal 1 there.

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=0\) into the rate formula.

parts.stem: Use integration to find an expression for \(V\) in terms of \(t\).
parts.hint: Integrate the rate and use the fact that the tank is empty at \(t=0\) to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Integrate the two exponential terms. The antiderivative of \(2e^{-t}\) is \(-2e^{-t}\).
The tank starts empty, so \(V(0)=0\). Substitute to find \(C\).
State the volume function.

parts.stem: Show that \(2e^{2t}-3e^t-2=0\) when \(V=3\).
parts.hint: Substitute \(V=3\) into the expression for volume, then multiply through by \(e^t\) to remove the negative exponent.

steps.explain: Set the volume formula equal to 3.
Multiply every term by \(e^t\).
Move all terms to one side.

parts.stem: Find \(t\), to the nearest minute, when \(V=3\).
parts.hint: Use the quadratic from part (iii) with \(u=e^t\), keep the positive solution, and convert the time from hours to minutes.

steps.explain: Let \(u=e^t\). The equation becomes a quadratic.
Since \(u=e^t>0\), take \(u=2\) and solve for \(t\).
Convert hours to minutes and round to the nearest minute.

questions.stem: The first snow of the season begins to fall during the night. The depth of snow, \(h\), increases at a constant rate through the night and the following day. At 6 am a snow plough begins to clear the road of snow. The speed, \(v\) km/h, of the snow plough is inversely proportional to the depth of snow: \(v=\frac{A}{h}\), where \(A\) is a constant. Let \(x\) km be the distance the snow plough has cleared and let \(t\) be the time in hours from the beginning of the snowfall. Let \(t=T\) correspond to 6 am.

parts.answer: Since snow depth increases at a constant rate from zero, h=ct for some constant c. Then dx/dt=v=A/h=A/(ct)=k/t, where k=A/c.
parts.stem: Explain carefully why, for \(t\geq T\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{k}{t}\), where \(k\) is a constant.
parts.hint: Write the constant rate of increase in snow depth as \(h=ct\). Then substitute this expression into \(v=A/h\), and use \(v=dx/dt\).

steps.explain: The snow depth starts at zero and increases at a constant rate, so it is proportional to time. Let \(h=ct\), where \(c\) is a positive constant.
The plough speed is the rate of change of distance, so \(v=dx/dt\). Substitute \(h=ct\) into the inverse-proportion rule.
Combine the constants by setting \(k=A/c\).

parts.stem: At what time did it begin snowing if the plough clears 1 km from 6 am to 8 am, then takes a further 3.5 hours to clear the next kilometre?

steps.explain: The first kilometre is cleared from \(t=T\) to \(t=T+2\). Integrate the speed law.
The next kilometre takes 3.5 hours, so it is cleared from \(T+2\) to \(T+5.5\). Its distance is also 1 km.
Equate the logarithms and solve for \(T\).
Convert \(8/3\) hours to 2 hours 40 minutes before 6 am.

steps.explain: 1. Domain
steps.work: \text{The function } f(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5 \text{ is a polynomial, so the domain is all real } x.

steps.explain: 2. Symmetry
steps.work: f(-x) = (-x)^2 - 4(-x) - 5 = x^2 + 4x - 5. \text{ This is neither } f(x) \text{ nor } -f(x)\text{, so it is neither even nor odd.}

steps.explain: 3. Intercepts and Sign
steps.work: \textbf{y-intercept:} f(0) = -5.\\ \textbf{x-intercepts:} \text{Set } y = 0 \implies x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0 \implies (x-5)(x+1) = 0 \implies x = -1 \text{ or } x = 5.

steps.explain: 4. Asymptotes
steps.work: \text{Since } f(x) \text{ is a polynomial, there are no vertical or horizontal asymptotes. As } x \to \pm\infty, y \to \infty.

steps.explain: 5. The first derivative
steps.work: y' = 2x - 4.\text{ Set } y' = 0 \implies x = 2.\\ \text{When } x=2, y = (2)^2 - 4(2) - 5 = -9. \text{ Stationary point at } (2, -9).\\ y' < 0 \text{ for } x < 2 \text{ (decreasing) and } y' > 0 \text{ for } x > 2 \text{ (increasing). Thus, } (2, -9) \text{ is a local minimum.}

steps.explain: 6. The second derivative
steps.work: y'' = 2.\text{ Since } y'' > 0 \text{ for all } x\text{, the curve is everywhere concave up. There are no points of inflection.}

steps.explain: 7. Any other features
steps.work: \text{The curve is a parabola opening upwards with its vertex at } (2, -9).

steps.explain: 1. Domain
steps.work: \text{The function } f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 \text{ is a polynomial, so the domain is all real } x.

steps.explain: 2. Symmetry
steps.work: f(-x) = -x^3 - 3x^2 + 4. \text{ This is neither even nor odd.}

steps.explain: 3. Intercepts and Sign
steps.work: \textbf{y-intercept:} f(0) = 4.\\ \textbf{x-intercepts:} \text{By testing factors of 4, } f(-1) = -1 - 3 + 4 = 0. \text{ Thus, } (x+1) \text{ is a factor.}\\ x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 = (x+1)(x^2 - 4x + 4) = (x+1)(x-2)^2.\text{ Intercepts at } x = -1 \text{ and } x = 2.

steps.explain: 4. Asymptotes
steps.work: \text{No asymptotes. As } x \to \infty, y \to \infty. \text{ As } x \to -\infty, y \to -\infty.

steps.explain: 5. The first derivative
steps.work: y' = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2).\text{ Set } y' = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } x = 2.\\ \text{When } x=0, y=4. \text{ When } x=2, y=0. \text{ Stationary points at } (0, 4) \text{ and } (2, 0).\\ \text{Using a table of slopes: } (0, 4) \text{ is a local maximum and } (2, 0) \text{ is a local minimum.}

steps.explain: 6. The second derivative
steps.work: y'' = 6x - 6 = 6(x - 1).\text{ Set } y'' = 0 \implies x = 1.\\ \text{When } x=1, y=2. \text{ The concavity changes from down } (y'' < 0) \text{ to up } (y'' > 0) \text{ at } x=1\text{, so } (1, 2) \text{ is a point of inflection.}

steps.explain: 7. Any other features
steps.work: \text{The } x\text{-intercept at } x=2 \text{ is also a stationary point, confirming it is a double root.}

steps.explain: 1. Domain

steps.explain: 2. Symmetry

steps.explain: 4. Asymptotes

steps.work: y' = 3x^2 - 6x - 24 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 8) = 3(x - 4)(x + 2).\text{ Set } y' = 0 \implies x = -2 \text{ or } x = 4.\\ \text{At } x = -2, y = 56 \implies (-2, 56) \text{ is a local maximum.}\\ \text{At } x = 4, y = -52 \implies (4, -52) \text{ is a local minimum.}

questions.stem: The curve \( y = ax^2 + bx + 5 \) has a turning point at \( (-2, 1) \). Find the value of the coefficient \( a \).
questions.hint: Set the derivative at x = -2 equal to 0, and plug the coordinate (-2, 1) into the curve equation.

steps.explain: Understand 'turning point'
steps.work: \text{A turning point at } (-2, 1) \text{ gives us two pieces of information: the point lies on the curve, and the derivative is zero at } x = -2.

steps.explain: Use the derivative condition
steps.work: \text{Differentiate the curve: } y' = 2ax + b.\\ \text{Set } y'(-2) = 0 \implies 2a(-2) + b = 0 \implies -4a + b = 0 \implies b = 4a.\\ \text{This is our first equation.}

steps.explain: Use the point condition
steps.work: \text{The point } (-2, 1) \text{ must satisfy the curve's equation. Substitute } x = -2 \text{ and } y = 1:\\ 1 = a(-2)^2 + b(-2) + 5 \implies 1 = 4a - 2b + 5 \implies 4a - 2b = -4.\\ \text{Dividing by 2 gives } 2a - b = -2.\\ \text{This is our second equation.}

steps.explain: Solve the simultaneous equations for a
steps.work: \text{Substitute } b = 4a \text{ from the first equation into the second equation:}\\ 2a - (4a) = -2 \implies -2a = -2 \implies a = 1

questions.stem: The curve \( y = ax^2 + bx + 5 \) has a turning point at \( (-2, 1) \). Find the value of the coefficient \( b \).
questions.hint: Use the relation b = 4a after finding a = 1.

Equation 2: Use the point condition
Solve the simultaneous equations for b
steps.work: \text{We have two equations:}\\ \text{1) } b = 4a\\ \text{2) } 2a - b = -2\\ \text{Substitute (1) into (2):}\\ 2a - (4a) = -2 \implies -2a = -2 \implies a = 1.\\ \text{Now substitute } a = 1 \text{ back into equation (1) to find } b:\\ b = 4(1) = 4

steps.work: \text{Convert the cube root into a fractional exponent:}\\ f(x) = x^{\frac{1}{3}}

steps.explain: Integrate using power rule
steps.work: \text{Increase the power by 1: } \frac{1}{3} + 1 = \frac{4}{3}\text{. Divide by } \frac{4}{3} \text{, which is equivalent to multiplying by } \frac{3}{4}:\\ \int x^{\frac{1}{3}} \, dx = \frac{x^{\frac{4}{3}}}{\frac{4}{3}} + C = \frac{3}{4}x^{\frac{4}{3}} + C

questions.stem:
Find the equation of the curve passing through the point \( (2, 4) \) with gradient function:
\( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 2 \)
questions.hint: Integrate gradient function to get family y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x + C, then plug in (2, 4).

steps.explain: Integrate the derivative to find the curve family
steps.work: \text{The equation of the curve } y \text{ is the integral of the gradient function } f'(x):\\ y = \int (3x^2 - 6x + 2) \, dx = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x + C

steps.explain: Substitute coordinates to solve for C
steps.work: \text{Since the curve passes through } (2, 4)\text{, substitute } x = 2 \text{ and } y = 4:\\ 4 = (2)^3 - 3(2)^2 + 2(2) + C\\ 4 = 8 - 12 + 4 + C \implies 4 = C

steps.explain: State final curve equation
steps.work: \text{Substitute } C = 4 \text{ back into the original equation:}\\ y = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x + 4

questions.stem: If \( f'(x) = 6x - 2 \) and \( f(2) = 11 \), find the value of \( f(3) \).
questions.hint: Integrate \(f'(x)\) to find f(x), solve for C with f(2) = 11, then calculate f(3).

steps.explain: Integrate derivative to get function f(x)
steps.work: \text{Find the primitive of } f'(x):\\ f(x) = \int (6x - 2) \, dx = 3x^2 - 2x + C

steps.explain: Substitute x = 2 and f(2) = 11 to solve for C
steps.work: \text{We are given } f(2) = 11:\\ 11 = 3(2)^2 - 2(2) + C\\ 11 = 12 - 4 + C \implies 11 = 8 + C \implies C = 3

steps.explain: State complete function f(x)
Evaluate f(3)
steps.work: \text{Substitute } x = 3 \text{ into the complete function:}\\ f(3) = 3(3)^2 - 2(3) + 3 = 27 - 6 + 3 = 24

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of A and B.
parts.hint: Differentiate and set the gradient equal to zero. Factor the quadratic to find both x-coordinates, then substitute each into the original curve.

steps.explain: Differentiate the cubic to get the gradient.

parts.hint: Concavity is determined by the second derivative. Find where it is positive.

steps.explain: Differentiate again to obtain the second derivative.

parts.stem: For what values of k does the equation x³ + x² − x + 2 = k have three real solutions?
parts.hint: Think of y=k as a horizontal line. It cuts the cubic three times only when its height is strictly between the local minimum and local maximum.

steps.explain: The graph has a local maximum of 3 at A and a local minimum of 49/27 at B.

steps.explain: A horizontal line between those two heights crosses the cubic once on each of its three branches. At either turning-point height, two intersections merge, so there are not three distinct solutions.
Therefore k must lie strictly between the turning-point y-values.
